                                                        Abstract
                The Sum of Square Roots (SSR) problem is the following computational problem: Given
                                                                                             Pk     √
            positive integers a1 , . . . , ak , and signs δ1 , . . . , δk ∈ {−1, 1}, check if i=1 δi ai > 0. The
            problem is known to have a polynomial time algorithm on the real RAM model of com-
            putation, however no sub-exponential time algorithm is known in the bit or Turing model
            of computation. The precise computational complexity of SSR has been a notorious open
            problem [GGJ76] over the last four decades. The problem is known to admit an upper
                                                                               PPPP
            bound in the third level of the Counting Hierarchy, i.e., PPP    and no non-trivial lower
            bounds are known. Even when the input numbers are small, i.e., given in unary, no better
            complexity bound was known prior to our work. In this paper, we show that the unary vari-
            ant (USSR) of the sum of square roots problem is considerably easier by giving a P/poly
            upper bound.


1           Introduction
The Sum of Square Roots problem (SSR) is the following computational                  problem: Given pos-
                                                                              Pk     √
itive integers a1 , . . . , ak , and signs δ1 , . . . , δk ∈ {−1, 1}, check if i=1 δi ai > 0. It was first
explicitly posed in an influential paper of Garey, Graham and Johnson [GGJ76] on NP-hardness
of geometric problems such as Euclidean TSP and Euclidean Steiner tree. They remark that
while such geometric problems are NP-hard “it is not at all apparent that this . . . is in NP”,
since comparing two given tours is reducible to SSR, which is not known to be in NP. In
fact, even when the input graph is presented via an embedding where vertices have integer co-
ordinates, the distance between vertices could still be irrational in the Euclidean metric. Hence
comparing lengths of two paths on such a graph, reduces to comparing two linear combina-
tions of square roots for which the best bounds we currently have seem to require exponential
precision [BFMS00]. However it has been often observed that in practice that a near-linear
bit-precision is sufficient to decide the sign of an SSR instance [SY17, Chapter 45], and it is
conjectured to be in P. SSR is an important subroutine in Computational Geometry where
many problems are known to be solvable in polynomial time relative to SSR [HS99]. We refer
the interested reader to [DMO06, KS12] and the references therein for a discussion on the status
of SSR and the stackexchange posts [Erib, Eria] for some interesting discussion on SSR-hard
problems and related geometric questions. Along with the more general problem, PosSLP1 ,
SSR has been frequently used as to show numerical hardness in diverse areas such as algorithmic
game theory [EY10, UW11, CIJ14], Semidefinite programming [Goe97], probabilistic verifica-
tion [EKL08, HK15, KW11, BLW13], formal language theory and logic [HKL17, LOW15].

Prior work
Garey et al. [GGJ76] attribute Andrew Odlyzko to the observation that approximating every
square root in the SSR instance by rational numbers with O(k2k ) bits and summing them up
suffices to infer the correct sign,P
                                   which yields an EXP upper bound for SSR. The main idea
                                          √
behind this observation is that ki=1 δi ai is an algebraic integer whose minimal polynomial
has degree at most 2k . Therefore by using standard root separation bounds (see Proposition 2),
one can infer the sign of any such algebraic integer by a suitable numerical approximation.
    Using the root separation bound, Tiwari [Tiw92] proved that SSR can be solved in polyno-
mial time on the unit cost arithmetic RAM model of computation via Newton iteration. Implicit
in Tiwari’s algorithm is an improved complexity bound: Newton iteration can be used to obtain
rational approximation to the square roots up to O(k2k ) bits, which can be represented as pair
of poly(k)-sized arithmetic circuits (for the numerator and the denominator). Evaluating such
circuits can be done in PSPACE. We now know from the work of Allender et al. [ABKPM09]
that Tiwari’s algorithm is essentially a polynomial time reduction from SSR to PosSLP, which
                       PPPP
places SSR in PPP         . This is currently the best known complexity upper bound for SSR.
A different algorithm achieving the same complexity bound, but via a reduction to matrix pow-
ering was presented in [ABD14]. All these results seem to inherently depend on root separation
bounds. Unfortunately, this line of attack on SSR has its limitations: there exist an integer
linear combination
              Pk √  of k square roots, whose minimal polynomial has degree exactly 2k ; Indeed
consider α = i=1 pi for distinct primes pi . It is well-known from Galois theory [ST01] that
the minimal polynomial of α has degree exactly 2k . Therefore we require fundamentally new
techniques to substantially improve the complexity of SSR.

Our work
Many authors have observed [GGJ76, Pap77] that Euclidean TSP is strongly NP-hard, i.e., the
problem is already NP-hard for those graphs where the co-ordinates of the graph are integers
of polynomially (in the number of vertices) bounded magnitude. This motivates                the following
                                                                                             √
variant, USSR : Given 1 ≤ a1 , . . . , ak ≤ k, and δ1 , . . . , δk ∈ {−1, 1}, test if ki=1 δi ai > 0. We

square roots in the example we constructed above, i.e., α = ki=1 pi are at most O(k log k).
Even for this simple “unary” variant, there is no better complexity upper bound known than

PPP          . In this work, we improve the state of affairs considerably. We show that

Theorem 1. USSR ∈ P/poly.

    We provide two proofs of Theorem 1, both yielding a P/poly (in fact even a TC0 /poly)
upper bound, which is tight modulo the non-uniformity since checking iterated addition of
integers is TC0 -hard. This is a strong indication that USSR should be decidable in P. One
consquence2 of our result is that USSR cannot be NP-complete unless the polynomial hierarchy
collapses to the second level. We would like to point out here that USSR is not a sparse 3
language: For every k where the instances of USSR have k positive integers from the range
{1, . . . k}, there could be potentially 2k distinct instances of USSR. Amazingly, there is still a
k O(1) -length advice string that non-trivially helps solve all the exponentially-many instances.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first instance of a natural (non-sparse) language that
can be solved in P/poly, but not known to be solvable in the polynomial hierarchy (PH).
  2
    However this consequence can be inferred by other means too: since SSR is closed under complement, if it
was also NP-complete, this would imply NP = coNP, collapsing the polynomial hierarchy.
  3
    If it were, then it would be trivially in P/poly

Related work
Cheng [Che06] studied the complexity of USSR and gave a subexponential time algorithm when
the integers in the instance are bounded by O(k log k) in magnitude. Kayal and Saha [KS12]
define an analogue of SSR for univariate polynomials and obtain an efficient algorithm for
deciding this variant. As a byproduct, they are able to show that SSR can be solved in P for
the closely related class of polynomial integers. The variant they solve is orthogonal to USSR
since there can be numbers of small magnitude that are not polynomial integers and vice versa.
Both SSR and USSR have been conjectured [Che06] to admit efficient algorithms, though there
has not been any concrete complexity-theoretic evidence before our work. A P      natural related
                                                                                         √
question, namely whether a sum of square roots can be checked for equality, i.e., ki=1 δi ai = 0
(as against SSR where one wants to infer the sign of the expression) can be solved efficiently
in P [Blo91].

3.1     Proof of Theorem 1 via Linear Threshold Functions
A Boolean function f : Bm → {±1} over a bounded discrete domain B is said to be a Linear
Threshold Function (LTF) if and P only if there exist real numbers w0 , w1 , . . . , wm ∈ R such that
for every x ∈ Bm , f (x) = 1 iff m   i=1 wi xi ≥ w0 . LTFs are central objects of study in many areas
of theoretical computer science such as circuit complexity, learning theory, analysis of Boolean
functions and communication complexity [AB09].
    The real numbers w0 , w1 , . . . , wm are said to be a realization of the LTF f . Note that any
LTF has infinitely many realizations. The following classical theorem due to Muroga [Mur65]
says that any LTF over a bounded discrete domain B, can also be realized with integer weights
of small 4 magnitude (i.e., representable using at most O(m log m)-bits). In fact the theorem
shows that such a representation is only dependent on m and the the maximum absolute value
of any element in the discrete bounded domain B. In particular it is independent of the real
numbers w0 , w1 , . . . , wm .

Theorem 7 (Muroga [Mur65]). Let b be the maximum magnitude of elements in B. For any
LTF f : Bm → {±1} realized using weights w0 , w1 , . . . , wm ∈ R, there exists an equivalent
integer realization with weights u0 , u1 . . . , um ∈ Z, where 1 ≤ |u0 |, . . . , |um | ≤ O((m + 1)!bm ).

   The proof of Theorem 7 follows from a simple application of Linear Programming and is a
fundamental result in Circuit Complexity and Learning Theory. We give an exposition of the
proof in the Appendix A for the sake of completeness. The proof of Theorem 1 is now immediate;

4     Summary and Conclusion
We have presented two non-uniform algorithms for USSR. Both can be viewed as “compress-
ing” exponentially many input instances into a polynomial-length advice string such that each
instance can be solved easily given the advice. Moreover, it is easy to see that the unary nature
of USSR does not play an important role here. In other words, given any set of k fixed positive
integers the corresponding 2k instances of SSR can be similarly compressed into a polynomial
length advice string from which extracting the solution to an instance is easy. In fact, the
compression is possible for the signed sum of any k fixed real numbers.

                                                  8
   A notable point about the numerical approximation proof is that the number of basis ele-
ments bi is only m + 1 while by the root separation bound their exponents ei are distributed
over an exponential range in m. Thus if the ei ’s are “well-distributed” i.e. consecutive ei ’s differ
by Ω(m2 ) then we just need to consult the value of one basis element to decide on an instance.
Prior to our work, there was no difference in the computational complexity between USSR and
SSR. Our work raises a few natural questions:

   1. Is there a polynomial time algorithm for USSR? Is there a way to use both the proofs in
      tandem to verify the advice? This would give an NP algorithm for USSR. Even a PH
      algorithm will be a significant improvement to the current state of affairs.

   2. Consider the proof via LTFs: Is it possible to estimate the number of vertices in the
      polytope of the LTF obtained from the UUSSR instance? Can we characterize when the
      vertices will be determined by easy UUSSR instances?

   3. Is it possible to eliminate either the values {vi }m                     m
                                                         i=0 or the basis {bi }i=0 from the advice
      string in the numerical approximation proof?

   4. Is SSR ∈ P/poly?

   5. Can reasoning similar to Remark 9 be used to give better bounds on distribution on roots
      of a univariate polynomial, or give improved root separation bounds?
